pricing.notes: 2026-27 season. Killington prices day tickets dynamically by date and publishes no fixed window rate, so all three ticket fields are null rather than guessed; the only public numbers are discounted rates (military $74-$165, Vermont/New Hampshire resident $69-$116). The unlimited adult season pass is tiered by purchase date: $1,339 through June 18 2026, $1,529 from June 19 to September 24, $1,899 from September 25. The figure recorded here is the rate on sale as of the verified date.

editorial.overview: Killington is the biggest ski area in the East and it never lets you forget it. Six peaks, 3,050 feet of vertical, and a lift network so sprawling that getting from Bear Mountain to Ramshead is a genuine commute — two rides and a traverse if you plan it well, three and a walk if you don't. The scale is real and so is the tradeoff: this is a mountain you have to learn, and first-timers routinely spend a day riding lifts instead of skiing. What Killington actually sells is season length. It opens before anyone else in the East, usually on a ribbon of manmade snow off the K-1 gondola in October, and it closes in late May or early June on Superstar, which by then is a white stripe running down an otherwise green mountain. Nobody else in New England can do that. The skiing in between is genuinely varied — Bear Mountain's steeps are the most serious lift-served pitch in Vermont, Snowdon and Ramshead are quiet intermediate cruising, and the Canyon quad accesses the best sustained fall line on the hill. The catch is that all of this is also true for the 8,000 other people who drove up from Boston, New York and Hartford, and Killington's parking, base area and lift queues have never fully caught up with its own popularity. Come midweek and it is arguably the best mountain in the East. Come on a February Saturday and you will spend a meaningful fraction of the day standing in a line at the gondola.
editorial.snowQuality: The 250-inch claim is believable at the summit and optimistic everywhere else — Killington's base is at 1,165 feet, low enough that the bottom third of the mountain sees rain in storms that fall as snow up top. The saving grace is a snowmaking plant that covers 600 acres and is genuinely the best in the East; Killington will rebuild a trail overnight and run guns into April when everyone else has given up. What that produces, though, is manmade snow, which after a thaw-freeze cycle turns into the hard, fast, blue-white surface that gives Vermont its reputation. Ski the top half after a natural storm and it is legitimately good. Ski the runouts to the K-1 base in late January and you are on machine-groomed hardpack, with the edges of every trail scraped to boilerplate by mid-morning.
editorial.crowds: Killington is the closest big mountain to three major metro areas, and on a Saturday it feels like it. The K-1 gondola is the single worst bottleneck — everyone parks at the main base and everyone rides it first, so the line peaks between 9:15 and 10:30 and can run 25 minutes. The Superstar and Snowdon six-packs absorb load better. The locals' move is to park at Skyeship on Route 4 and ride up from there, which skips the K-1 scrum entirely, or to start at Bear Mountain and work back. Ikon changed the texture of the crowds more than the volume: more out-of-state day-trippers, more first-time visitors who don't know the mountain, and a noticeably busier midweek than a decade ago. April is its own phenomenon — the Superstar spring scene draws a party crowd that has very little to do with skiing, and if that is not what you came for, avoid the last three weekends of the season.
editorial.difficulty: Killington's ratings run honest to slightly soft by Eastern standards. A blue here is a real blue, and the greens off Ramshead are genuinely gentle, which makes it a better learning mountain than its reputation suggests. Where self-described intermediates get in trouble is Bear Mountain: Outer Limits is the steepest sustained bump run in the East and it is rated double black for a reason, but the singles around it are rated black and are still far steeper and icier than the blues you warmed up on. The other trap is the glades, which are marked as if they are ordinary trails and are frequently unskiable early season because the underbrush is not buried yet. Compared to the West, everything is shorter, narrower and harder underfoot — a Killington black is not a Utah black, it is a firmer, tighter, more technical version of one.

keyTrails.name: Superstar
keyTrails.note: The reason Killington skis into June. The resort points a disproportionate share of its snowmaking at this one trail, builds a base measured in feet, and lets it melt out slower than anything else in the East. It is also a legitimately good steep pitch in midwinter, and a zoo in April.

keyTrails.name: Outer Limits
keyTrails.note: Advertised as the steepest mogul trail in the East, and for once the marketing is not overstating it. Wide, relentless, visible from the Bear Mountain quad so everyone watches you ski it. Bumps set up hard by late morning.

keyTrails.name: Cascade
keyTrails.note: The best sustained intermediate fall line on the mountain and the answer to 'where do I go when K-1 is a madhouse'. Long, consistent pitch off Snowdon with far less traffic than the Superstar side.

keyTrails.name: Juggernaut
keyTrails.note: Roughly six miles from Killington Peak to the Skyeship base — the longest run in Vermont and more of a novelty tour than a ski run. Mostly a green-rated cat track, but it is the one way to actually feel the size of the place.

keyTrails.name: Devil's Fiddle
keyTrails.note: Bear Mountain's other serious pitch. Steeper than it looks from the lift, holds bumps, and empties out fast once the Outer Limits crowd commits.

tidbits: Killington and neighbouring Pico are sold as one resort on the Ikon Pass, and a day at both counts as a single day against your allotment.
Killington Peak tops out at 4,241 feet, making it the second-highest summit in Vermont after Mount Mansfield.
The snowmaking system covers 600 acres and can move nine million gallons of water a day.
The resort's own stats page reports Killington and Pico combined, which is why most third-party sites quote 1,977 acres and 213 trails for what people actually mean by 'Killington'.
bestFor: The longest season in the East
watchOutFor: Rain at the base when it snows up top
The April party scene on Superstar

reviews.gist: Rates Killington the top mountain in Vermont and the strongest all-round option on the East Coast, chiefly on size and snowmaking. Its main complaint is logistical: the mountain is awkward to navigate and moving between areas often costs several lift rides.

Fourth in the East, behind three northern-Vermont mountains that all out-snow it. On a system weighted toward snow quality, the biggest ski area in the East does not finish first — which is a fair summary of the argument about Killington.

moguls.policy: Bear Mountain is the bump pod and is managed as one: Outer Limits is left ungroomed as policy for most of the season rather than being seeded, and the surrounding singles are groomed only intermittently. Everything on the Snowdon and Ramshead side is groomed nightly, so the bumps are concentrated in one corner of a very large mountain.

namedRuns.name: Outer Limits
namedRuns.note: The canonical Eastern bump run and the longest and steepest of them. Wide enough to hold several lines, and fully visible from the Bear Mountain quad, so there is always an audience.

namedRuns.name: Devil's Fiddle
namedRuns.note: Bear Mountain's other serious pitch. Bumps up when it is left alone, which is most of midwinter, and empties out once the Outer Limits crowd commits.

namedRuns.name: Superstar
namedRuns.note: Groomed for most of the winter, but the spring bumps that form on it in late April and May are the reason the mogul crowd stays until June.

moguls.quality: The Outer Limits line is genuinely good by Eastern standards - the pitch is consistent enough that the troughs form a rhythm rather than a random field, and the trail is wide enough that a second and third line develop through the weekend. The failure mode is ice. After a thaw-freeze the troughs glaze and the bumps go from firm to unskiable, and because Killington makes so much snow the surface underneath is manmade and sets up harder than natural pack. Skier consensus is consistent that it is best in spring and worst in a dry January.
moguls.bestTiming: Late March through the April spring cycle, when the base is deep and the surface softens by mid-morning. Midwinter the bumps are there but frequently firm; the week after a real storm is the other window.
moguls.bumpCulture: The strongest bump scene in the East. The Bear Mountain Mogul Challenge has run on Outer Limits since 1981 and is now as much a spring party as a competition - a single-run qualifier with head-to-head sudden-death finals, age divisions from youth to 50-plus, held in early April.

parks.name: Reason Park
parks.note: The first park to open each season, often the first in the country. Lapped from the North Ridge Quad, with fresh setups built daily.

parks.name: Full House
parks.note: A line of small features for learning, set next door to Mouse Run so the step up is one traverse away.

parks.name: Mouse Run Park
parks.note: The signature Snowdon-area park, off the Snowdon Six Express, running medium to large features.

parks.name: Timberline Park
parks.note: Killington Parks' crown jewel - a 1,000-foot-long run packed with jumps, rails, transitions and creative features, off the Ramshead Express Quad.

parks.name: Lil' Stash
parks.note: The little brother of Bear Mountain's Stash, on Ramshead. Wooden and natural features at a scale beginners can actually use.

parks.name: Easy Street
parks.note: Mellow boxes and small features. The bottom rung of the progression ladder.

parks.name: Dream Maker
parks.note: Large freestyle features, and the top of the ladder that starts at Easy Street.

parks.name: The Stash
parks.note: Freestyle riding in the woods on Bear Mountain, built with Burton, with over 60 natural features. Unlike anything else in the East.

parks.progression: A deliberate ladder rather than a collection: Easy Street and Full House for learning, Reason and Mouse Run in the middle, Dream Maker and Timberline at the top. The Stash sits outside it as a tree-park in its own right.
parks.rebuildCadence: Reason Park is rebuilt daily - the resort describes fresh setups every day - and the parks crew works the network all season rather than building once and letting it decay.
parks.overview: The largest park network in Vermont and one of the few in the East built as a genuine progression rather than one flagship park plus an afterthought. Eight parks spread across four pods means you can spend a day in them without repeating yourself.
parks.reputation: Regionally strong and consistently rated near the top in the East, though Mount Snow’s Carinthia is the benchmark for sheer scale. The Stash is the differentiator - very few mountains anywhere run a Burton tree park, and it is the thing park riders mention first about Killington.
